strengths: Addresses a novel and timely problem: image knowledge copyright protection in multimodal RAG-as-a-Service, which is indeed underexplored compared to text-only RAG watermarking.

Two complementary watermarking strategies (acronym-based and spatial-relationship-based) are well-motivated by differing OCR/spatial reasoning capabilities across VLMs, providing some flexibility for black-box deployment.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two datasets (MMQA, WebQA) and four VLM generators (LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL3, Qwen-VL-Chat, Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct), covering effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, and robustness.
Statistical verification framework using Welch's t-test and clearly defined metrics (Rank, CGSR, VSR, SimScore) gives a rigorous quantitative basis for watermark detection claims.

Robustness tests against common image transformations (rescale, rotate, Gaussian blur) and query-efficiency comparison against baselines (Naive, Opt.) show the method requires fewer queries to reach statistical significance.

Ablation-style experiments (PCA visualization, retrieval ratio vs. watermark number, relevant-query harmlessness tests) add useful supporting evidence to the paper's stealthiness and harmlessness claims.
weaknesses: The core watermarking techniques are conceptually simple (embedding an OCR-readable text string or an unusual spatial arrangement into a synthetic image), which is a fairly straightforward extension of existing text/image generation tools rather than a fundamentally new watermarking mechanism; novelty is more in the application/combination than in the underlying technique.

Stealthiness claims rely mainly on embedding-space similarity (PCA, low unintended retrieval rate) but do not address a natural and simple adversarial defense: an adversary could run OCR or object-anomaly detectors over the knowledge base to flag/filter images containing suspicious embedded text (AQUA_acronym) or implausible scene compositions (AQUA_spatial), which seems like an easy and effective countermeasure that is not evaluated.

Robustness evaluation is limited to generic image transformations (rescale, rotate, Gaussian blur) and does not test targeted removal attacks specifically designed against the watermark signal (e.g., text-region inpainting/cropping for acronym watermarks, or object removal/replacement for spatial watermarks).

The reference distribution values used for real-world deployment (Appendix B) appear to be fixed illustrative numbers rather than derived systematically, raising questions about how practical and generalizable the proposed real-world verification protocol actually is.

The method and evaluation are restricted to the T2T (text-to-text) multimodal RAG subclass; generalization to other multimodal RAG architectures (e.g., text-and-image-to-image) is left entirely to future work, limiting the scope of the contribution.

The threat model assumes the defender can freely craft arbitrary secret acronyms/spatial scenes and that the adversary does not attempt any content sanitization or moderation of ingested data, which may be optimistic relative to real RaaS deployments that often include content filtering.

Limited discussion of watermark scalability and quality control when generating large numbers of watermark images via LLM/diffusion pipelines, including potential collisions, low-quality generations, or detectability patterns that might emerge at scale.

No comparison to more sophisticated or recent watermarking baselines beyond the two self-constructed baselines (Naive and PGD-based Opt.), which may not represent the strongest possible adversarial detection or attack scenario.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously unexplored gap: prior RAG watermarking work (WARD, RAG©, RAG-WM, DMI-RAG) is text-only, and this paper is the first to target image knowledge in multimodal RAG.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical protocol spanning four VLM generators (LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL3, Qwen-VL-Chat, Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct) and two datasets (MMQA, WebQA), with dedicated experiments for effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, and robustness.
Statistically grounded verification procedure using Welch's t-test and clearly defined metrics (Rank, CGSR, SimScore, VSR) that could be reused by follow-up work.

The two proposed mechanisms (acronym-based OCR triggers, spatial-relationship cues) are simple, cheap to generate at scale via LLM/diffusion models, and intuitively map image semantics onto detectable textual outputs.
weaknesses: Core stealthiness claim is questionable: AQUA_acronym embeds an explicit, prominent text string (the acronym) directly into the image (see Fig. 3, Table 4 examples), which is trivially detectable by a human glance or a simple OCR-based content filter looking for embedded text/acronyms—an adaptive adversary filtering images containing overlaid text would likely defeat the method entirely, yet this obvious removal/filtering threat is not tested or discussed.

The 'imperceptible to users' claim is only supported by embedding-space PCA visualization and retrieval-rate statistics; no human perceptual study was conducted to substantiate that watermark images look natural to actual viewers, despite this being one of the paper's four core design goals.

Baselines are weak and not representative of the state of the art: 'Naive' is just random ordinary images (not really a watermarking method), and 'Opt.' is a generic PGD adversarial-patch approach not designed for retrieval-based multimodal settings; no comparison is made against adapted versions of the very text-watermarking works discussed in Related Work, nor against any stronger recent optimization-based image watermark with retrieval considerations.

The 'Real-world Deployment' protocol (Appendix B) that relies on comparing a suspect system's single (mean, variance) against precomputed reference distributions for 'clean' and 'watermarked' systems is under-specified and somewhat circular—how a defender obtains reliable clean/watermarked reference statistics without already having full access to a comparable system is not clearly justified, and only one illustrative example distribution is given rather than a principled estimation procedure.

Robustness evaluation is limited to basic rescale/rotate/Gaussian-blur transforms; there is no evaluation against more realistic and threatening manipulations such as JPEG compression, cropping, larger perturbation budgets, generator fine-tuning, or retriever/encoder replacement, all of which are plausible adversary actions given the stated threat model.

The threat model assumes the defender can issue effectively unlimited probe queries (up to hundreds per experiment) without being rate-limited, monitored, or blocked by the RaaS provider; this practical constraint on real-world query budgets/costs is not addressed.

Detection guarantees are only evaluated under the assumption the adversary ingests the entire watermarked knowledge base; partial or subsampled reuse of the base (a very plausible adversarial strategy) is not analyzed, weakening the claimed reliability of copyright tracing.

Novelty of the underlying technique is somewhat limited—embedding readable text for OCR-based extraction and using unusual object co-occurrence for VQA-style extraction are fairly straightforward applications of existing VLM capabilities rather than a substantially new watermarking mechanism.

Sampling temperature is fixed at a relatively high T=1.2 for all experiments; the sensitivity of CGSR/VSR to more standard/lower-temperature or greedy decoding (which many production RAG deployments would use) is not explored, leaving open whether reported success rates generalize to realistic deployment settings.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored problem: watermarking image knowledge for copyright protection in multimodal (T2T) RAG-as-a-Service systems, whereas prior RAG watermarking work is text-only.

Clear articulation of the unique technical challenges of multimodal watermarking (indirect propagation from retriever to generator, unapparent pixel-level distribution shift, need for explicit rather than implicit detectability) compared to plain-text RAG and traditional image watermarking.
Two complementary, well-motivated methods (acronym-based for OCR-capable VLMs, spatial-relationship-based for others) that together broaden applicability across different generator capabilities.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: 4 VLM generators, 2 datasets, statistical hypothesis testing (Welch's t-test) for principled verification, and evaluation across effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, and robustness axes.

Useful auxiliary analyses such as TPR/FPR curves, query-efficiency-to-significance comparison against baselines, PCA embedding visualization, and retrieval-ratio-vs-watermark-count experiments that support the stealthiness/effectiveness claims from multiple angles.
Reasonable baseline comparisons (naive real-image watermark and PGD-based imperceptible perturbation) showing AQUA's advantages in query efficiency and effectiveness.
weaknesses: The core techniques are conceptually simple (embedding literal acronym text or generating an absurd/surreal scene via off-the-shelf diffusion models); the novelty is more in problem framing and evaluation methodology than in fundamentally new watermarking mechanisms.

Stealthiness claims rely mainly on CLIP-embedding PCA overlap rather than human perceptual studies or targeted detectors; watermark images (large acronym text overlays, obviously surreal spatial scenes like a dragon lighting candles) seem plausibly easy for a human reviewer or an OOD/anomaly filter to flag, which is not tested — no adaptive-adversary evaluation is provided.

Robustness evaluation is limited to basic transformations (rescale, rotate, Gaussian blur); more realistic adversary defenses such as cropping, JPEG compression, near-duplicate/OOD filtering, or re-captioning/re-generation of the knowledge base are not evaluated, despite the threat model explicitly considering an adversary that might try to filter suspicious content.

Reproducibility is weakened: the code link in the paper is left blank/incomplete, and the "real-world deployment" reference-distribution numbers (Appendix B) appear to be illustrative placeholders rather than derived from a principled or general procedure.
Only a single retriever (CLIP ViT-L/14) is evaluated; generalization of the method's retrieval/rank behavior to other embedding models or retrieval strategies is untested.

Scale of watermark images tested (50 per method) is relatively small, and there is limited analysis of how watermark quality/diversity affects performance at larger scale or under adversarial dataset curation.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., typo "AQUAarconym" section heading, some notation inconsistencies) suggest the manuscript could benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practical problem: no prior work watermarks image knowledge in Multimodal RAG-as-a-Service, filling a clear gap relative to text-only RAG watermarking methods.

Two complementary, well-motivated watermarking mechanisms (acronym-based OCR triggers and spatial-relationship cues) that are designed to survive indirect (image-to-text) watermark propagation, a genuinely distinct challenge from prior image watermarking or text RAG watermarking.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 4 generator VLMs, 2 datasets, and multiple model scales (2B-38B), with principled statistical verification (Welch's t-test, Z-test, hypothesis testing framework) rather than only point-estimate detection rates.

Thorough coverage of all four stated design goals (effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, robustness), including PCA stealthiness analysis, adaptive VLM-based filtering adversaries, WAVES-benchmark image transformation/regeneration attacks, retriever replacement/fine-tuning, corpus scaling, and adversarial fine-tuning to suppress watermark responses.
Reasonable baselines (naive common-image watermark and PGD-based optimization watermark) that highlight AQUA's superior query efficiency and detection reliability.
Good reproducibility support: code released, public datasets used, detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and additional qualitative examples.

Practical discussion of real-world deployment issues (reference distribution estimation, multi-provider watermark collision avoidance) that shows awareness of deployment realism beyond a narrow lab setting.
weaknesses: The threat model assumes the defender can freely inject synthetic watermark images into a proprietary dataset and craft arbitrary probe queries with known ground-truth signatures; whether real data providers would accept modifying their datasets with fabricated images is not deeply discussed, and could raise questions about knowledge-base integrity/utility beyond the tested QA benchmarks.

AQUA_acronym and AQUA_spatial both rely on model capabilities (OCR and spatial/compositional reasoning) that could vary substantially across future or non-English VLMs; generalization to weaker or specialized (e.g., domain-specific, non-VLM) RAG generators is not evaluated.

The 'Opt.' PGD baseline is a somewhat weak/non-specialized comparator for this setting (imperceptible adversarial perturbation baselines are typically designed for classification, not VLM instruction following), so the large performance gap over baselines may partly reflect baseline mismatch rather than purely AQUA's advantage.

Stealthiness claims rest partly on PCA visualization and VLM-filter FPR/TPR trade-offs; a human perceptual study or more rigorous statistical distinguishability test (beyond PCA and a single VLM filter) is absent, leaving open whether sophisticated or multimodal forensic detectors could still discriminate watermark images.

The spatial method’s reliance on 'improbable scenes' (e.g., apple on a dog's head) could, in principle, be noticeable to human curators or downstream users even if VLM filters struggle, and this human-in-the-loop risk is not empirically tested.

Watermark collision avoidance across multiple data providers is discussed only qualitatively/theoretically (Appendix B.2) without empirical validation of the proposed centralized registry or combinatorial verification claims.

Robustness experiments use attack 'strength' fixed at 1 in the WAVES benchmark; it is unclear how AQUA performs under stronger degradations or more adaptive attacks that specifically target the geometric/semantic cues (e.g., object removal or scene rearrangement attacks tailored to spatial watermarks).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and previously unstudied gap: watermarking of image knowledge in multimodal RAG-as-a-Service systems, whereas prior RAG watermarking work is text-only.

Two complementary watermark constructions (acronym-based OCR trigger for models with strong OCR, spatial-relationship trigger for models with weaker OCR) are sensibly motivated by the identified challenge of 'indirect watermark propagation' from image retriever to text generator.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two datasets (MMQA, WebQA), four VLM generators, and a battery of robustness tests (WAVES image-level attacks, retriever replacement/fine-tuning, large-scale corpus drift, adversarial LoRA fine-tuning, frontier-model refusal checks).

Statistically grounded verification protocol (Welch's t-test, two-proportion Z-test, reference-distribution estimation for real-world deployment) adds methodological rigor beyond simple accuracy reporting.
Reasonable harmlessness and stealthiness analysis (PCA embeddings, adaptive VLM-based filtering, FPR under scaling watermark counts) that at least attempts to probe an adaptive adversary.
Code and detailed appendices are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical idea is conceptually a canary/steganographic hidden-QA-pair trick (embed a secret text or scene relationship, later query it via OCR/VQA) rather than a fundamentally new or provably robust watermarking mechanism; novelty is largely in the application setting rather than the method itself.

The paper's own adaptive-filter experiment (Table 12) shows a trivial 'does this image contain text' OCR filter achieves 100% TPR against AQUA_acronym; the paper dismisses this by citing high FPR (61-72%) on benign images, but does not test a more targeted adaptive attack (e.g., flagging out-of-dictionary/nonsense capitalized acronyms), which could plausibly achieve much lower FPR while still catching the watermark—leaving a real robustness gap unaddressed.

AQUA_spatial relies on deliberately unusual/improbable object relationships, which is in tension with the paper's claim of 'unapparent distribution shift'; the same adaptive-filter experiment shows some non-trivial detection (2-4% TPR) for this method, suggesting it is not fully stealthy against scrutiny.

Baselines are weak: the 'Naive' baseline (random unrelated images) is a strawman with no real chance of success, and the 'Opt.' adversarial-perturbation baseline is not representative of stronger classical/robust image watermarking or steganographic techniques (e.g., StegaStamp-style approaches) that could have served as more meaningful points of comparison.

Key evaluation metrics (SimScore, harmlessness judgments) rely on an LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro) without validation against human annotation, raising concerns about metric reliability and potential self-serving bias in reporting extremely favorable numbers (e.g., p-values of 0.0).

Full effectiveness pipeline (CGSR/Rank across the main experiments) is only evaluated on moderately sized open-source VLMs (7B-38B); frontier closed models (Gemini-3-Pro, GPT-5.1, Qwen3-VL) are only checked for refusal behavior, not for full watermark detectability, leaving open whether the method generalizes to the most capable/most likely production-grade RAG generators.

The threat model implicitly assumes the adversary is unaware of the specific watermarking scheme (security through obscurity); once the scheme (acronym text or unusual object pairing) becomes publicly known—as it would after publication—an adversary has a fairly well-defined signature to search for and filter, which is a common weakness of the approach not deeply engaged with.

strengths: Addresses a clearly identified and practically important gap: no prior work has tackled copyright watermarking for image knowledge in multimodal RAG-as-a-Service systems, which is well-motivated by the increasing deployment of multimodal RAG.

Proposes two complementary, well-designed watermarking strategies (acronym-based and spatial-relationship-based) that target different generator capabilities (strong OCR vs. limited OCR), making the framework flexible across black-box deployment scenarios.

Very comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning four generator VLMs (LLaVA-NeXT, InternVL3, Qwen-VL-Chat, Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct), two datasets (MMQA, WebQA), and model scales from 2B to 38B parameters, demonstrating broad applicability.

Rigorous statistical verification methodology, including Welch's t-test and two-proportion Z-test for hypothesis testing, plus a well-thought-out real-world deployment protocol (reference distribution estimation) that accounts for the practical constraint that defenders typically cannot observe both clean and watermarked statistics simultaneously.

Thorough assessment across all four stated design goals (effectiveness, harmlessness, stealthiness, robustness), including PCA visualization, adaptive VLM-based filtering attacks, image-level transformation/regeneration attacks (WAVES benchmark), adversarial fine-tuning attacks, and system-level changes (retriever replacement, large-scale dataset drift).
Includes sensible baselines (naive common-image watermark and an optimization-based PGD watermark) that clearly show AQUA's superior query efficiency and detection reliability.
Good reproducibility practices: code released, datasets public, detailed appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and extended qualitative examples.

Robustness evaluation against frontier models (Gemini-3-Pro, GPT-5.1-High, Qwen3-VL) and explicit testing against refusal behavior and adversarial fine-tuning shows genuine effort to stress-test the method against realistic adaptive adversaries.
weaknesses: Limited baseline diversity: the only substantive external comparison is a self-constructed optimization-based (PGD) watermark; no comparison to any other emerging multimodal or cross-modal watermarking technique, partly because none may exist, but this leaves the magnitude of the advance somewhat self-referential.

Effectiveness depends heavily on the generator's OCR/VLM reasoning ability; CGSR for smaller models (e.g., 2B-parameter models) is noticeably lower (~70-92%) than larger models, which could be a limitation precisely for smaller/less capable unauthorized RAG providers that copyright holders may most want to catch.

The AQUA_spatial watermark images are generated via diffusion models, which could in principle be distinguishable from real dataset images using AI-generated-image forensics tools; this potential stealthiness vulnerability is not evaluated.

Evaluation is restricted to two QA-style multimodal datasets (MMQA, WebQA); generalization to other domains (e.g., medical, e-commerce, document-heavy corpora) claimed as motivation in the introduction is not empirically tested.

The practical hypothesis-testing framework (Appendix B.1) relies on reference distributions that must be estimated per RAG system/dataset combination, which could be difficult for a defender without visibility into the suspect system's generator/retriever choice; the provided "conservative" generic thresholds are only loosely justified.

Only one adversarial fine-tuning attack configuration is tested (LoRA + NEFTune on a single model); more diverse or stronger adaptive attacks (e.g., distillation, different fine-tuning objectives, watermark-aware retrieval filtering) are not explored, so robustness claims may be somewhat overstated.

Dense notation and multiple overlapping metrics (Rank, CGSR, VSR, SimScore, p-values) make the methodology section and tables somewhat hard to parse; a consolidated summary or more intuitive explanation would improve clarity.
